description: FLARECRAFT is a team that tackles the topics people tend to overlook: forest fires, air quality, and how to combine seemingly unrelated datasets into accurate predictions. We believe science and fun aren’t opposites, so every project we build turns real data into something people actually want to explore, learn from, and share.
summary: GeoFlare turns NASA's fire satellites into answers people can act on: which fires could turn severe, how fire has really changed since 2003, and whether the air is safe near gas flares and factories. MODIS and VIIRS count the same fires very differently, so a stitched record shows a false 3.6x jump in 2012. We trained a model that translates MODIS into VIIRS units cell by cell and week by week, and tested it honestly by hiding each year in turn. Our AI severity model, trained on 77 million NASA FIRMS detections from 2025 and 2026 with same-day NASA POWER weather, gives every fire burning today a 0-100 Fire Risk Score. On the newest months it catches 86% of severe fires (10 MW or more), and 78% of fires it rates Extreme really were severe. GeoFlare Air finds the gas flares and factories that the same satellites see glowing in one spot all year. It joins them with live air quality and the wind into a plain verdict and step-by-step precautions for that day's air. Flick, our mascot, guides every page and answers questions from the real data.
details:
What it does. GeoFlare answers three questions from NASA satellite data: which of today's fires could turn severe, how fire has really changed in a place since 2003, and is the air safe where I live? It has two apps in one site, with Flick, a small flame with a satellite in orbit, as narrator and guide.

1. The AI severity model (GeoFlare Fires, Now). Every fire NASA FIRMS reports in the last 24 hours (VIIRS NOAA-20 or NOAA-21) is scored for its chance of being severe: a fire radiative power of 10 MW or more.

- What it uses: a CatBoost model trained on 2025 and 2026 detections. It reads each fire's brightness, pixel size, confidence, time of day, season and place, plus the same-day NASA POWER humidity, rain and soil wetness, and a dryness index built from them.

- Trained to miss as little as possible: a missed severe fire costs more than a false alarm, so the threshold is set to catch severe fires first.

- A score anyone can read: the probability is calibrated into a 0-100 Fire Risk Score (Low, Medium, High, Extreme).

- How good it is, on months it never saw (29 June to 13 November 2026): ROC-AUC 0.89. It catches 86% of severe fires. 78% of fires rated Extreme were really severe; of fires rated Low, only 5%.

- Still useful with gaps: it was trained with missing inputs too, so a forecast that knows only the place and date still gets a sensible score.

- In the app: the map shows mild, maybe and likely-severe fires. Flick checks each score against the fire power the satellite measured. A 4-week outlook combines a place's usual fire season with the model's severity chance. Anyone can tap the map to score a fire of their own.

2. Air quality next to fires and flares (GeoFlare Air). Type a town or share your location.

- Factories and flares, from the satellites: GeoFlare finds the gas flares, refineries and factories within 100 km in the same NASA archive. These are hotspots that glow in the same place week after week, which FIRMS marks as static sources and we keep separate from wildfires. For each one it shows the distance, the direction, how many weeks it glowed, its trend since 2012, and whether it is glowing today (live FIRMS).

- The air and the wind: GeoFlare adds today's air quality (US AQI, PM2.5, PM10, NO2, SO2, CO, ozone), each pollutant against the WHO 24-hour guideline, and the wind. It tells you whether the brightest nearby site is upwind of you right now.

- A plain verdict: the higher of the air-quality band and an industry level. The industry level is high when a site is within 10 km, or within 30 km with the wind blowing its smoke toward you.

- What to do: animated step-by-step precautions for that level of air (such as closing windows and doors), following US EPA AirNow advice.

- The big picture: a world map of every factory and flare that glowed in 2026, and the countries where they glow most.

3. The harmonized fire record (GeoFlare Fires, Past). This answers the challenge.

- The model: gradient boosting on MODIS counts (Terra and Aqua separately), fire power, neighbouring cells and each cell's fire regime, trained on the years both sensors flew. It translates MODIS into VIIRS units and rebuilds 2003-2011 with 80% uncertainty bands.

- Validated honestly, one held-out year at a time: 33% median monthly error against 35% for a single factor, better in 12 of 14 years, with 80% of true values inside the 80% bands.

- 2026 so far: added from NOAA-20, converted to Suomi NPP units with their measured ratio (0.996).

- For any place: a fire calendar from 2003 to 2026, the fire season, unusual months, a long-term trend with a significance test, a week-by-week map, a CSV export and a country leaderboard.

- The archive tab: every 2025 and 2026 detection on a map, scored by the model.

Ask Flick: a chat that answers questions about the fires, the air and the model through read-only tools over our data, so its numbers come from the data.

How the data flows. A Python pipeline cleans 77 million NASA FIRMS detections (MODIS and VIIRS, 2025 and 2026) and joins each one to the nearest same-day NASA POWER weather point. NASA's near-real-time months have no hotspot type, so we label them from static heat sources seen earlier that year. Back-tested, this catches 92% of factories and flares and mislabels 0.6% of fires.

Benefits and impact.

- Fire crews and agencies can see which of today's fires to look at first.

- People who live next to oil fields and industry get a daily, plain-language air check with clear steps.

- Trends are finally comparable across the 2012 sensor change, so a real increase can be told apart from a sharper camera.

- Every number comes with an honest range.

Tools.

- Python (pandas, scikit-learn, CatBoost, DuckDB, FastAPI), with PostgreSQL/PostGIS or a CSV fallback.

- D3.js, Leaflet and anime.js for the interface; Power BI for the 2025 dashboard.

- Docker, Airflow and GitHub Actions.

- A ready-to-run Windows release: double-click GeoFlare.exe and Flick asks what to open.

Creativity.

- Gas flares turned from noise in the fire data into a health signal.

- A mascot who narrates the science, points at what he talks about and speaks.

- A story that opens with the 2012 mystery and lets you guess.

Factors we considered.

- Honesty over hype: the harmonization gain over one fixed factor is modest, and we say so.

- The severity model scores fires that are already detected; it does not predict where fires start.

- Air values are model estimates (Copernicus CAMS), not a sensor at your door, and the app says so.

- Detections are not burned area.

- Everyday language and accessibility (reduced motion, keyboard use).
